| **During the session**          | Self-assessments feel honest (a spread of ratings, not all 3s)                                                                                                                                                       |
|                                 |                                                                                                                                                                                                                      |
|                                 | Priority gaps are specific and actionable                                                                                                                                                                            |
|                                 |                                                                                                                                                                                                                      |
|                                 | The team gap map reveals internal expertise that was not previously visible                                                                                                                                          |

| **Within 2-4 weeks**            | Someone starts working on a priority gap (accessing a resource, practising a skill, asking a colleague for help)                                                                                                     |
|                                 |                                                                                                                                                                                                                      |
|                                 | The manager references the gap map when assigning work or development opportunities                                                                                                                                  |
|                                 |                                                                                                                                                                                                                      |
|                                 | An internal peer learning opportunity emerges from the 'Who Could Teach It' column                                                                                                                                 |

| **CLOVER ERA data (4-6 weeks)** | Learning pillar scores increase                                                                                                                                                                                      |
|                                 |                                                                                                                                                                                                                      |
|                                 | Qualitative data references development, growth, or skills                                                                                                                                                           |
|                                 |                                                                                                                                                                                                                      |
|                                 | Opportunity scores may also improve (visible development paths increase engagement)                                                                                                                                  |

| **Red flags**                   | If the diagnostic produces a nice grid but nobody acts on it, the exercise created awareness without action. Connect priority gaps to specific next steps using L6 (Accountability) and L7 (Real-World Application). |

## Cross-Pillar Connections

  **Worksheet**                    **Connection**                                                                                        **Direction**

  **L2: Peer-to-Peer Learning**    The 'Who Could Teach It' column in L1 directly feeds L2's session design.                          Run L1 before L2

  **L4: Learning Resources**       L1 identifies WHAT to learn; L4 identifies HOW to learn it.                                           Run L1 before L4

  **L6: Accountability**           L6 builds the accountability structure to ensure L1's priority gaps get addressed.                   Run L1 then L6

  **L7: Real-World Application**   L7 ensures learning translates to work. L1 identifies the learning; L7 bridges it to practice.        Complementary

  **OP1: Ambition Roadmap**        Skills gaps connect to career aspirations. L1 provides the skills data; OP1 provides the direction.   Complementary

worksheets.title: Peer-to-Peer Learning Sessions
worksheets.forWhat: Lack of cross-team learning, uneven skill development, low engagement in formal learning programs, no culture of continuous learning
worksheets.lede: - Schedule sessions at a regular cadence (biweekly works well; weekly is too frequent for most teams)
worksheets.body:
# L2: Peer-to-Peer Learning Sessions

**Pillar**          **Learning**                                                         **Difficulty**           **Level 1**

  **Time Required**   45-60 minutes (per session)                                          **Group Size**           4-10

  **Mode**            Team facilitation                                                    **Format**               In-person or remote

  **Prerequisites**   L1 (Skills Diagnostic) recommended to identify topics and teachers   **CLOVER ERA Trigger**   Lack of cross-team learning, uneven skill development, low engagement in formal learning programs, no culture of continuous learning

## Why This Works

| **THE NEUROSCIENCE**                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              |
|                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   |
| Social learning activates the brain's mirror neuron system. When we learn from a peer rather than a textbook or video, the brain engages empathy circuits alongside learning circuits. The result is deeper encoding: information learned from someone we know and trust is retained more effectively than information from an anonymous source. |
|                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   |
| Teaching is also one of the most powerful learning mechanisms for the teacher. The act of organising knowledge for presentation forces the brain to restructure and deepen its own understanding (the "protege effect"). Peer learning creates a double benefit: the learner gains knowledge and the teacher consolidates expertise.            |
|                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   |
| The dopamine system also responds differently to peer learning. Learning from a colleague who faced the same challenges provides a progress signal: 'If they can do it, so can I.' This is more motivating than learning from an expert whose competence feels unreachable.                                                                     |

## The Exercise

### Phase 1: Topic and Teacher Matching (first session only, 10 minutes)

Using the team gap map from L1, identify the first 2-3 peer learning sessions:

-   Match a skill gap with a team member who has expertise in that area

-   Confirm the teacher is willing and comfortable (do not volunteer people without asking)

-   Schedule sessions at a regular cadence (biweekly works well; weekly is too frequent for most teams)

| **FACILITATION NOTE**                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                           |
|                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                 |
| The teacher does not need to be an expert. They need to know more than the learners and be willing to share what they know. Framing matters: "You're the most experienced person on this team in \[skill\]. Would you be willing to run a 30-minute session sharing what you've learned?" is more effective than "Can you teach a class?" |

### Phase 2: Session Structure (ongoing sessions, 45 minutes)

Each peer learning session follows a consistent structure:

  **Time**      **Phase**          **What Happens**

  0-5 min       Context            Teacher explains why this skill matters and where it shows up in the team's work. Connects to real examples.

  5-20 min      Core Teaching      Teacher shares their approach, demonstrates techniques, walks through a real example. Not a lecture. Conversational, with questions encouraged throughout.

  20-35 min     Practice           Learners try applying the skill to a real or realistic scenario. Teacher coaches in real time. This is where the actual learning happens.

  35-45 min     Debrief            What clicked? What's still unclear? What will you try this week? Each person names one specific application.

| **WHAT TO SAY (MANAGER, AT THE START OF EACH SESSION)**                                                                                                                                                                                                         |
|                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                 |
| "This is not a formal training. This is \[Name\] sharing what they know because they've been doing it well and the rest of us can learn from them. Interrupt, ask questions, disagree. The best learning happens in the conversation, not the presentation." |

### Phase 3: Follow-Up Application

Between sessions, each learner applies one thing from the session to their actual work. At the start of the next session, 5 minutes for quick check-ins: "What did you try? What worked? What didn't?" This creates a learning-practice-feedback loop that dramatically improves retention.

## Facilitation Notes

  **Situation**                                          **Response**

  **The teacher over-prepares and delivers a lecture**   Coach beforehand: "The goal is 50% teaching, 50% practice. If you find yourself talking for more than 15 minutes straight, pause and give people something to try." Most internal teachers default to lecture mode because that's what they've experienced in formal training.

  **Attendance drops after the first 2-3 sessions**      This usually means sessions aren't relevant enough or the application phase isn't happening. Ask: "Are these topics still your priority gaps?" and "Are you finding opportunities to use what you're learning?" Adjust topics based on current team needs.

  **Nobody wants to be the teacher**                     This is a vulnerability issue. Teaching exposes you to questions you might not be able to answer. Normalise it: "You don't need to know everything. You just need to know more than the rest of us about this topic. And it's completely fine to say 'I don't know, let me find out.'"

## Signs This Is Working

| **Timeframe**                   | **What to Look For**                                                                |

| **During sessions**             | Learners ask questions and challenge the teacher's approach                        |
|                                 |                                                                                     |
|                                 | The practice phase produces visible learning ("Oh, I see how that works now")     |
|                                 |                                                                                     |
|                                 | Sessions feel like conversations, not presentations                                 |

| **Between sessions**            | Learners apply what they learned and report back                                    |
|                                 |                                                                                     |
|                                 | The teacher's own understanding deepens from preparing and responding to questions |
|                                 |                                                                                     |
|                                 | Team members reference skills learned in peer sessions during regular work          |

| **CLOVER ERA data (4-8 weeks)** | Learning scores increase                                                            |
|                                 |                                                                                     |
|                                 | Cross-team learning signals improve                                                 |
|                                 |                                                                                     |
|                                 | Qualitative data references colleagues teaching, sharing, or developing together    |

## Cross-Pillar Connections

  **Worksheet**                    **Connection**                                                                                                               **Direction**

  **L1: Skills Diagnostic**        L1 identifies the topics and teachers. L2 activates them.                                                                    Run L1 before L2

  **L7: Real-World Application**   L7 ensures peer learning translates to work. The follow-up application phase in L2 is a lightweight version of L7.           Complementary

  **V2: Failure Stories**          Teaching requires vulnerability. V2's normalisation of failure makes it safer to teach (and to not know all the answers).   V2 supports L2

worksheets.title: Learning Journal
worksheets.forWhat: No culture of continuous learning, learning not embedded in daily workflow, fear of failure in learning, low engagement in learning programs
worksheets.lede: Choose a format (physical notebook, digital note, app). The format matters less than the habit. Provide three daily prompts:
worksheets.body:
# L3: Learning Journal

**Pillar**          **Learning**                                      **Difficulty**           **Level 1**

  **Time Required**   15 minutes setup, then 5 minutes daily            **Group Size**           Individual (with optional team sharing)

  **Mode**            Solo (manager self-work or individual practice)   **Format**               Any

  **Prerequisites**   None                                              **CLOVER ERA Trigger**   No culture of continuous learning, learning not embedded in daily workflow, fear of failure in learning, low engagement in learning programs

## Why This Works

| **THE NEUROSCIENCE**                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                     |
|                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          |
| The brain's default mode network (DMN) processes and consolidates learning during periods of reflection. Without deliberate reflection, learning experiences pass through working memory and are rapidly forgotten. The forgetting curve (Ebbinghaus) shows that without reinforcement, 70% of new information is lost within 24 hours. |
|                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          |
| Writing activates different neural circuits than thinking alone. The act of putting learning into words forces the brain to organise, categorise, and connect new information to existing knowledge. This process, called elaborative encoding, substantially increases retention and the ability to apply learning in new contexts.     |

## The Exercise

### Phase 1: Setup (15 minutes, once)

Choose a format (physical notebook, digital note, app). The format matters less than the habit. Provide three daily prompts:

| **DAILY JOURNAL PROMPTS**                                                                                          |
|                                                                                                                    |
| 1\. What did I learn today? (A skill, a piece of information, something about a colleague, something about myself) |
|                                                                                                                    |
| 2\. Where did I struggle today? (Not to dwell on it, but to identify where growth is happening)                    |
|                                                                                                                    |
| 3\. What will I do differently tomorrow based on today? (One specific thing, not a general aspiration)             |

The third prompt is the most important. It converts reflection into action. Without it, the journal becomes a diary rather than a learning tool.

### Phase 2: Weekly Review (10 minutes, weekly)

Once a week, read the week's entries. Look for patterns: recurring struggles (same gap showing up?), progress on priority skills, connections between different learning moments. Write one sentence summarising the week's most important learning.

### Phase 3: Team Sharing (optional, 5 minutes in team meeting)

| **WHAT TO SAY**                                                                                                                                                                              |
|                                                                                                                                                                                              |
| "Who has a learning insight from this week they'd be willing to share? Not a polished lesson. Something you noticed, something that surprised you, something you're still figuring out." |

Keep this voluntary and brief. The goal is to normalise continuous learning as visible team behaviour, not to create a performance obligation.

## Facilitation Notes

  **Situation**                                                                **Response**

  **People stop after a week**                                                 The habit fails most often because 5 minutes feels like 'one more thing.' Anchor it to an existing routine: "Do it in the last 5 minutes before you close your laptop for the day." Habit stacking (attaching a new habit to an existing one) is the most reliable behaviour change technique.

  **Entries become performative ("I learned that teamwork is important")**   Push for specificity: "What specifically about teamwork? What moment today showed you something about how you or someone else collaborates?" Generic entries produce no learning. Specific entries produce insight.

## Cross-Pillar Connections

  **Worksheet**               **Connection**                                                                                                                     **Direction**

  **R1: Micro-Reflection**    L3 is a learning-specific reflection practice. R1 provides broader reflection prompts. They can share the same daily habit slot.   Complementary (combine or alternate)

  **L1: Skills Diagnostic**   Journal entries often surface skill gaps that the L1 diagnostic missed.                                                            L3 feeds back into L1 over time

  **V2: Failure Stories**     The 'where did I struggle' prompt builds the self-awareness that makes V2's failure sharing more genuine.                       Complementary

worksheets.title: Learning Resources and Engagement
worksheets.forWhat: Overwhelmed by too many resources, lack of accessible learning tools, low engagement in learning programs, decision fatigue around development options
worksheets.lede: Most people are surprised by the count. Then the reality check: "Of those, how many have you actively used in the last month?" The gap between available and used is usually enormous.
worksheets.body:
# L4: Learning Resources and Engagement

*Merged worksheet. Absorbs L5 (Organising Learning Tools) and L8 (Making Learning Relevant and Engaging). This is now the single worksheet for selecting, organising, and engaging with learning resources.*

  **Pillar**          **Learning**                                       **Difficulty**           **Level 1**

  **Time Required**   35-45 minutes                                      **Group Size**           4-12 or individual

  **Mode**            Team facilitation or solo                          **Format**               In-person or remote

  **Prerequisites**   L1 (Skills Diagnostic) to identify what to learn   **CLOVER ERA Trigger**   Overwhelmed by too many resources, lack of accessible learning tools, low engagement in learning programs, decision fatigue around development options

## Why This Works

| **THE NEUROSCIENCE**                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  |
|                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                       |
| Decision fatigue is neurologically real. Each decision the brain makes depletes the same cognitive resources used for learning. When employees face 50 learning options without guidance on which ones matter, the brain's response is often paralysis: no decision is made, no learning happens. This is the paradox of choice applied to professional development. |
|                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                       |
| Engagement with learning resources is also a dopamine question. Resources that match the learner's preferred format, connect to real work challenges, and provide visible progress signals keep dopamine flowing. Resources that feel irrelevant, passive, or disconnected from work produce no reward signal, and the brain abandons them.                          |

## The Exercise

### Phase 1: Resource Audit (10 minutes)

| **WHAT TO SAY**                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                |
|                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                |
| "How many learning resources do you currently have access to? Count everything: company training platforms, online courses you've bookmarked, books on your shelf, podcasts in your queue, mentoring relationships. Write down every resource you could theoretically use for development." |

Most people are surprised by the count. Then the reality check: "Of those, how many have you actively used in the last month?" The gap between available and used is usually enormous.

### Phase 2: The Three-Filter Sort (10 minutes)

For each resource on the list, apply three filters in order:

1.  Relevance: does this directly address one of my L1 priority gaps? (Yes/No)

2.  Format fit: does this match how I actually learn? (If you learn by doing and the resource is a 40-hour video course, it's a mismatch regardless of quality.)

3.  Time reality: can I realistically engage with this in the next month given my workload? (Yes/No)

Resources that pass all three filters go on the active list. Everything else goes on the 'future' list or gets cut entirely. The goal is to reduce the active list to 2-3 resources maximum.

### Phase 3: Engagement Design (10 minutes)

For each resource on the active list, design the engagement:

-   When will I use it? (specific day/time, anchored to existing routine)

-   How will I make it active, not passive? (take notes, practise the skill, discuss with a colleague, apply to a real project)

-   What's my progress marker? (not 'finish the course' but 'be able to do X that I couldn't do before')

| **FACILITATION NOTE**                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  |
|                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        |
| The progress marker question is the most important. "Complete the course" is a completion metric, not a learning metric. "Be able to build a pivot table without looking up the steps" is a competence metric. The brain responds to competence gains with dopamine. It responds to completion with a brief satisfaction spike that quickly fades. |

### Phase 4: Team Resource Sharing (5 minutes)

Go round the team: each person names their top resource and why they chose it. This creates a team knowledge base of recommended resources and often surfaces options that people didn't know existed.

## Facilitation Notes

  **Situation**                                                    **Response**

  **Someone has no learning resources available**                  This is an enablement issue, not a learning issue. "That's worth flagging. Let's identify what you need and I'll work on getting access." Connect to E5 (Access to Technology/Resources) if this is a systemic problem.

  **The team's learning platform is mandated but poorly rated**   Acknowledge reality: "If the mandatory platform isn't working for people, that's useful data. Let's separate what's required from what's effective, and supplement the required training with resources that actually help."

## Cross-Pillar Connections

  **Worksheet**                    **Connection**                                                                    **Direction**

  **L1: Skills Diagnostic**        L1 identifies WHAT to learn. L4 identifies HOW to learn it efficiently.           Run L1 before L4

  **L6: Accountability**           L4 selects the resources; L6 builds the structure to ensure they get used.        Run L4 then L6

  **L7: Real-World Application**   L4's engagement design should connect directly to L7's application framework.   Complementary

  **E5: Technology/Resources**     If resource access is the barrier, E5 addresses the enablement gap.               Use E5 for systemic access issues

worksheets.title: Accountability in Learning
worksheets.forWhat: Low accountability for learning, learning goals set but not followed through, no visible learning progress, leaders not modelling learning behaviours
worksheets.lede: Pair team members. Each pair commits to a weekly 5-minute check-in (in person, Slack, or at the start of an existing meeting). The check-in has exactly two questions:
worksheets.body:
# L6: Accountability in Learning

**Pillar**          **Learning**                                                                        **Difficulty**           **Level 1**

  **Time Required**   35-40 minutes                                                                       **Group Size**           4-10 or pairs

  **Mode**            Team facilitation                                                                   **Format**               In-person or remote

  **Prerequisites**   L1 (Skills Diagnostic) and L4 (Learning Resources) to provide goals and resources   **CLOVER ERA Trigger**   Low accountability for learning, learning goals set but not followed through, no visible learning progress, leaders not modelling learning behaviours

## Why This Works

| **THE NEUROSCIENCE**                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                             |
|                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  |
| Accountability leverages the brain's social commitment circuitry. When a goal is stated publicly or shared with an accountability partner, the brain treats it differently than a private intention. Social commitment activates the prefrontal cortex's planning systems and creates a social reward/consequence signal: the dopamine reward of reporting progress and the cortisol cost of having to explain why you didn't follow through. |
|                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  |
| The most effective accountability structures are lightweight, frequent, and reciprocal. A weekly 2-minute check-in with a learning partner produces better outcomes than a quarterly formal review because the brain responds to frequent feedback loops, not infrequent evaluations.                                                                                                                                                            |

## The Exercise

### Phase 1: Learning Contract Design (15 minutes)

Each person creates a Learning Contract with four elements:

4.  The skill I'm developing (from L1 priority gaps)

5.  The resource I'm using (from L4 active list)

6.  My progress marker (specific, observable competence gain, not a completion metric)

7.  My commitment cadence (how much time per week and when)

| **CALIBRATION**                                                                                                                                                 |
|                                                                                                                                                                 |
| Too ambitious: "I'll spend 2 hours every day studying data analytics." (Unsustainable with a full workload.)                                                 |
|                                                                                                                                                                 |
| Right level: "I'll spend 20 minutes every Tuesday and Thursday morning practising SQL queries using real team data." (Specific, bounded, connected to work.) |
|                                                                                                                                                                 |
| Too vague: "I'll try to learn more about project management." (No resource, no time, no marker.)                                                             |

### Phase 2: Accountability Pairing (10 minutes)

Pair team members. Each pair commits to a weekly 5-minute check-in (in person, Slack, or at the start of an existing meeting). The check-in has exactly two questions:

-   "Did you do what you committed to this week?" (Binary: yes or no. No elaborate explanations.)

-   "What's your commitment for next week?" (Specific and bounded.)

| **FACILITATION NOTE**                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                |
|                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      |
| The binary yes/no is deliberate. It prevents the common accountability failure where people explain at length why they didn't follow through, receive sympathetic understanding, and then repeat the pattern. "No" is a complete and acceptable answer. The follow-up question is about the future, not the past. |

### Phase 3: Manager's Role (5 minutes)

| **WHAT TO SAY**                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                               |
|                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                               |
| "My role in this is not to police your learning. It's to remove barriers. If your accountability check-in reveals that you're consistently unable to find the time, that's a workload problem, not a motivation problem. Bring that to me and we'll solve it together." |
|                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                               |
| "I'm also going to model this. My learning contract is \[share yours\]. My accountability partner is \[name\]. I'll report on my progress alongside everyone else."                                                                                                       |

## Facilitation Notes

  **Situation**                                               **Response**

  **Accountability pairs stop checking in after 2-3 weeks**   This is the most common failure. Prevention: schedule the check-ins into the calendar at the outset, not as a 'we'll find time' arrangement. If the habit dies, restart with a simpler commitment: "Just text each other on Friday: did you or didn't you? One word."

  **Someone consistently reports 'no' without distress**    The learning goal may not be genuinely important to them, or the commitment is misaligned with their reality. Revisit L1: "Is this still your priority gap? If not, what is?" The contract should change rather than persist as a source of comfortable failure.

## Cross-Pillar Connections

  **Worksheet**                     **Connection**                                                                                                                     **Direction**

  **L1: Skills Diagnostic**         L6 holds people accountable for developing the priority gaps identified in L1.                                                     Run L1 before L6

  **L4: Learning Resources**        L6 ensures the resources selected in L4 actually get used.                                                                         Run L4 before L6

  **R3: Reflection Buddy System**   The accountability pairing model is similar to R3. Teams can use the same pairs for both learning and reflection accountability.   Complementary

  **V11: Workload Struggles**       If accountability failures are workload-driven, V11 provides the framework for surfacing and addressing capacity issues.           Use V11 if workload is the barrier

worksheets.title: Real-World Application
worksheets.forWhat: Learning doesn't translate to real-world application, low engagement in learning programs, skills developed in training but not visible in work
worksheets.lede: The gap is usually stark. People recall 5-10 learning experiences but identify 1-2 where they applied the content. This is not a personal failure; it is a transfer design failure. Name it as such.
worksheets.body:
# L7: Real-World Application

*Rebuilt from scratch. The original offered generic advice. This version provides a specific transfer design methodology.*

  **Pillar**          **Learning**                                          **Difficulty**           **Level 2**

  **Time Required**   40-50 minutes                                         **Group Size**           4-10

  **Mode**            Team facilitation                                     **Format**               In-person or remote

  **Prerequisites**   L1 (Skills Diagnostic) and active learning underway   **CLOVER ERA Trigger**   Learning doesn't translate to real-world application, low engagement in learning programs, skills developed in training but not visible in work

## Why This Works

| **THE NEUROSCIENCE**                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                           |
|                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                |
| The gap between learning and doing is called the transfer problem, and it is the single biggest waste in corporate training. Research consistently shows that without deliberate transfer design, less than 20% of learning content is applied in the workplace. The brain stores training knowledge in episodic memory ("I learned this in a workshop") rather than procedural memory ("I do this automatically in my work"). Transfer design moves learning from episodic to procedural. |
|                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                |
| The brain encodes skills through deliberate practice, not through exposure. Watching a video on negotiation skills does not develop negotiation skills. Practising negotiation with real feedback does. The 70-20-10 model reflects this neuroscience: 70% of learning happens through experience, 20% through social interaction, and 10% through formal training. Most learning investment goes into the 10% that produces the least transfer.                                               |

| **IF A TEAM MEMBER ASKS "WHY ARE WE DOING THIS?"**                                                                                                                                                              |
|                                                                                                                                                                                                                   |
| "Most of what people learn in training never makes it into their actual work. This exercise bridges that gap by identifying specific, real opportunities to apply new skills in the work we're already doing." |

## The Exercise

### Phase 1: The Learning-Doing Gap Audit (10 minutes)

| **WHAT TO SAY**                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  |
|                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  |
| "Think about everything you've learned in the past 6 months. Training, courses, workshops, reading, coaching. How much of it have you actually applied in your work? Be honest. Write down what you learned and, next to each item, whether you've used it." |

The gap is usually stark. People recall 5-10 learning experiences but identify 1-2 where they applied the content. This is not a personal failure; it is a transfer design failure. Name it as such.

### Phase 2: Application Mapping (15 minutes)

For each priority gap from L1, create a specific application plan:

  **Skill**       **Current Project**   **Specific Application**   **When**          **How I'll Know It Worked**

  *\[From L1\]*   *\[Real work\]*       *\[Exact task\]*           *\[This week\]*   *\[Observable result\]*

The "Specific Application" and "When" columns must be concrete. "Use communication skills in meetings" is not an application. "Use the SBI feedback framework in Thursday's 1:1 with Sarah" is an application.

### Phase 3: Implementation Intentions (10 minutes)

Research on implementation intentions (Gollwitzer, 1999) shows that framing plans as "When X happens, I will do Y" doubles follow-through compared to general intentions.

| **WHAT TO SAY**                                                                                                                                                                                         |
|                                                                                                                                                                                                         |
| "For your most important application, frame it as a when-then plan: 'When \[specific trigger situation\], I will \[specific new behaviour\].' Write it on a card. Put it somewhere you'll see it." |

Examples:

-   "When I'm about to send a complex email, I will apply the three-point simplification from C11."

-   "When a team member raises a problem in standup, I will practise active listening for 60 seconds before responding."

-   "When I finish a task, I will write two sentences in my learning journal before moving to the next one."

### Phase 4: Follow-Up Design (5 minutes)

Schedule a follow-up check-in (2-4 weeks out) where each person reports: did you apply it? What happened? What would you do differently? This closes the loop and makes the application visible to the team.

## Facilitation Notes

  **Situation**                                                               **Response**

  **Applications are vague or generic**                                       Push for specificity: "Which project? Which meeting? Which day? If you can't name the context, the brain won't activate the skill when the moment arrives." Vague applications produce zero transfer.

  **Someone says they have no opportunity to apply what they're learning**   Two possibilities: the learning is not relevant to their current work (revisit L1 and L4), or they don't recognise the opportunities (help them map: "Tell me about your next week. Where could this skill show up?"). The second is more common.

## Signs This Is Working

| **Timeframe**                   | **What to Look For**                                                                                       |

| **During the session**          | Application maps are specific and connected to real work                                                   |
|                                 |                                                                                                            |
|                                 | Implementation intentions feel concrete, not aspirational                                                  |
|                                 |                                                                                                            |
|                                 | People can identify the trigger situation for their when-then plan                                         |

| **Within 2-4 weeks**            | At least one person reports successfully applying a new skill                                              |
|                                 |                                                                                                            |
|                                 | The follow-up check-in produces real stories of application (and productive stories of failed application) |
|                                 |                                                                                                            |
|                                 | Someone says "I used the thing we practised"                                                             |

| **CLOVER ERA data (4-6 weeks)** | Learning scores increase                                                                                   |
|                                 |                                                                                                            |
|                                 | Qualitative data references applying, using, or practising new skills                                      |
|                                 |                                                                                                            |
|                                 | Productivity-related indicators may improve as applied skills produce results                              |

## Cross-Pillar Connections

  **Worksheet**                   **Connection**                                                                                                                 **Direction**

  **L1: Skills Diagnostic**       L7 applies the priority gaps identified in L1 to real work.                                                                    Run L1 before L7

  **L2: Peer-to-Peer Learning**   Peer sessions produce knowledge; L7 converts it to application. The follow-up check-in in L2 is a lightweight version of L7.   Complementary

  **L6: Accountability**          L6 holds people accountable; L7 provides the specific application targets to be accountable for.                               Run together

  **R2: From Ideas to Action**    R2 addresses the broader challenge of converting insight into behaviour change. L7 is the learning-specific version.           Complementary

worksheets.title: Tracking Learning Progress
worksheets.forWhat: Lack of feedback on learning progress, no visible outcome from learning, leaders not tracking development
worksheets.lede: Each person creates a simple, personal learning dashboard. Format does not matter (notebook, spreadsheet, sticky note on the monitor). Content matters:
worksheets.body:
# L9: Tracking Learning Progress

**Pillar**          **Learning**                                                **Difficulty**           **Level 1**

  **Time Required**   30-35 minutes setup, then 5 minutes weekly                  **Group Size**           Individual or team

  **Mode**            Solo or team facilitation                                   **Format**               Any

  **Prerequisites**   L1 and L6 (to provide goals and accountability structure)   **CLOVER ERA Trigger**   Lack of feedback on learning progress, no visible outcome from learning, leaders not tracking development

## Why This Works

| **THE NEUROSCIENCE**                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   |
|                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        |
| The dopamine system responds to progress signals, not just completion. Each visible marker of advancement triggers a small dopamine release that reinforces the learning behaviour. This is why games use progress bars, experience points, and level-ups: they make progress visible to the brain's reward system. Learning without visible progress feels like running on a treadmill. The effort is real but there is no forward motion to reward. |
|                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        |
| Tracking also activates the brain's metacognitive systems. When people review their own progress, the prefrontal cortex engages in self-regulation: comparing actual against intended, identifying where effort is needed, and adjusting strategy. Without tracking, this self-regulation does not happen and learning drifts.                                                                                                                        |

## The Exercise

### Phase 1: Progress Dashboard Design (15 minutes)

Each person creates a simple, personal learning dashboard. Format does not matter (notebook, spreadsheet, sticky note on the monitor). Content matters:

  **Skill (from L1)**   **Starting Point**                 **Current Level**      **Target (with date)**

  *\[Priority gap\]*    *\[Where I was when I started\]*   *\[Updated weekly\]*   *\[Where I'm aiming by when\]*

The "Starting Point" is essential. Without a baseline, progress is invisible. "I couldn't build a pivot table in January. I can now build one with filters and calculated fields" is a visible, motivating progression.

### Phase 2: Weekly Update Ritual (5 minutes weekly)

Once a week, update the "Current Level" column. Ask: "What can I do now that I couldn't do last week?" If the answer is 'nothing,' either the learning effort is not producing results (adjust the approach) or the progress is happening but is not visible yet (look harder).

### Phase 3: Manager Check-In Integration (ongoing)

| **WHAT TO SAY (IN 1:1s)**                                                                                                                                                                                                   |
|                                                                                                                                                                                                                             |
| "Show me your learning dashboard. Where are you seeing progress? Where are you stuck? What do you need from me?" Three questions. Two minutes. This signals that learning matters enough for the manager to ask about it. |

If the manager never asks about learning progress, the team will correctly conclude that learning is a lower priority than task completion. Regular check-ins prevent this.

## Signs This Is Working

| **Timeframe**                   | **What to Look For**                                                               |

| **During setup**                | Dashboards have specific, measurable starting points and targets                   |
|                                 |                                                                                    |
|                                 | People can articulate what progress looks like for their priority gap              |

| **Within 4-6 weeks**            | Dashboards are being updated (even if progress is slow)                            |
|                                 |                                                                                    |
|                                 | At least one person can point to a visible competence gain                         |
|                                 |                                                                                    |
|                                 | The manager regularly asks about learning progress in 1:1s                         |

| **CLOVER ERA data (4-8 weeks)** | Learning scores increase                                                           |
|                                 |                                                                                    |
|                                 | Qualitative data references progress, growth, or development                       |
|                                 |                                                                                    |
|                                 | Engagement indicators may also improve (visible development is a retention signal) |

## Cross-Pillar Connections

  **Worksheet**               **Connection**                                                                                      **Direction**

  **L1: Skills Diagnostic**   L1 provides the skills and starting points. L9 tracks movement from those starting points.          Run L1 before L9

  **L6: Accountability**      L6 provides the check-in structure; L9 provides the data for those check-ins.                       Run together

  **OP1: Ambition Roadmap**   Learning progress connects to career progression. L9 data can feed into OP1 career conversations.   Complementary

worksheets.title: Equitable Learning Opportunities
worksheets.forWhat: Inconsistent learning opportunities across departments, unequal access to development, some team members getting more training/mentoring than others
worksheets.lede: Create a simple grid: team members on one axis, learning opportunity types on the other. Mark who received what. The patterns are usually visible immediately: certain people receive disproportionate investment, and it often correlates with proximity to the manager, tenure, or role visibility rather than development need.
worksheets.body:
# L10: Equitable Learning Opportunities

**Pillar**          **Learning**                                                                       **Difficulty**           **Level 2**

  **Time Required**   40-50 minutes                                                                      **Group Size**           5-12

  **Mode**            Team facilitation (manager-led, with honest self-assessment)                       **Format**               In-person or remote

  **Prerequisites**   L1 (Skills Diagnostic) to surface patterns in who gets development opportunities   **CLOVER ERA Trigger**   Inconsistent learning opportunities across departments, unequal access to development, some team members getting more training/mentoring than others

## Why This Works

| **THE NEUROSCIENCE**                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    |
|                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                         |
| Perceived unfairness triggers a strong threat response. Neuroscience research shows that the brain processes inequity through the same circuits it uses for physical pain (the anterior insula). When employees perceive that others receive more development opportunities, it produces a cortisol response that erodes trust and engagement, even if the employee's own opportunities are adequate in absolute terms.                                                                                                |
|                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                         |
| Equity in learning is also a neuroplasticity issue. The brain's ability to develop new skills does not stop at a certain career stage, seniority level, or role type. When organisations concentrate learning investment in high-performers or high-potentials, they create a self-fulfilling prophecy: those who receive development develop, and those who don't receive it stagnate. The gap widens not because of innate capability but because of differential access to neuroplasticity-activating experiences. |

## The Exercise

### Phase 1: The Access Audit (10 minutes)

| **WHAT TO SAY**                                                                                                                                                                                                                                             |
|                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                             |
| "I want us to look honestly at how learning opportunities are distributed on this team. In the last 6 months, who has attended external training, been mentored, been given a stretch assignment, or received dedicated development time? Let's map it." |

Create a simple grid: team members on one axis, learning opportunity types on the other. Mark who received what. The patterns are usually visible immediately: certain people receive disproportionate investment, and it often correlates with proximity to the manager, tenure, or role visibility rather than development need.

### Phase 2: The Honest Conversation (15 minutes)

| **WHAT TO SAY**                                                                                                                                                                                |
|                                                                                                                                                                                                |
| "Let's look at this map honestly. Is this distribution fair? If not, what's driving the imbalance? I'm asking because some of this is probably my doing, and I need to see it to fix it." |

Common drivers: the manager defaulting to the same people for stretch assignments, some team members being more vocal about requesting development, part-time or remote workers being overlooked, assumptions about who is 'ready' for development based on current performance rather than potential.

| **FACILITATION NOTE**                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          |
|                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                |
| This exercise requires the manager to accept accountability for distribution patterns without becoming defensive. If the map shows inequity, the correct response is: "I see this. Some of it was intentional but some of it wasn't. Let me explain the intentional decisions and commit to changing the unintentional patterns." Defending the status quo will shut down the conversation. |

### Phase 3: Rebalancing Plan (15 minutes)

The team creates a rebalancing plan:

-   Who hasn't received a learning opportunity recently and what would benefit them most?

-   How can stretch assignments be rotated rather than defaulting to the same people?

-   What structural changes would make learning access more equitable? (e.g., a learning budget per person rather than per team, explicit rotation of conference attendance, mentoring available to all levels)

The manager commits to specific changes with timelines. "I'll ensure everyone has at least one development opportunity in the next quarter" is a commitment. "I'll try to be more equitable" is not.

## Facilitation Notes

  **Situation**                                                                                  **Response**

  **The map reveals that the manager has invested most heavily in one or two people**            Own it directly: "I see the pattern. Some of this was because \[honest reason\]. Going forward, here's what I'm committing to change." Do not rationalise. The team can see the pattern regardless of the explanation.

  **A team member says they don't want or need development opportunities**                      Explore gently: "That's fine if it's genuine. But sometimes people stop asking because they've learned that asking doesn't produce results. Is it that you don't want development, or that you've given up expecting it?" The distinction matters.

  **The team identifies organisational barriers (budget, policy) that the manager can't fix**   Separate what the manager controls from what they don't. "I can't change the training budget. But I can change how I allocate stretch assignments, who gets mentoring access, and how I distribute the budget we do have. Let's focus on what's in our control."

## Signs This Is Working

| **Timeframe**                   | **What to Look For**                                                               |

| **During the session**          | The access audit produces honest patterns, not a sanitised picture                 |
|                                 |                                                                                    |
|                                 | The manager accepts accountability without defensiveness                           |
|                                 |                                                                                    |
|                                 | The rebalancing plan has specific names, actions, and dates                        |

| **Within 4-8 weeks**            | A team member who previously received no development opportunity gets one          |
|                                 |                                                                                    |
|                                 | Stretch assignments are visibly rotated                                            |
|                                 |                                                                                    |
|                                 | The manager proactively offers development rather than waiting for requests        |

| **CLOVER ERA data (6-8 weeks)** | Learning scores improve across the team (not just for previously favoured members) |
|                                 |                                                                                    |
|                                 | Equity-related signals improve                                                     |
|                                 |                                                                                    |
|                                 | Engagement may increase for team members who previously felt overlooked            |

## Cross-Pillar Connections

  **Worksheet**                  **Connection**                                                                                                                   **Direction**

  **L1: Skills Diagnostic**      L1 identifies who needs what development. L10 ensures the distribution is equitable.                                             Run L1 before L10

  **OP2: Opportunity Mapping**   Equitable learning connects to equitable career opportunities. L10 addresses the learning side; OP2 addresses the career side.   Complementary

  **V1: Vulnerability Circle**   Honest conversation about equity requires trust. V1 builds the safety L10 needs.                                                 V1 before L10 for low-trust teams

Learning Pillar Summary

The complete Learning pillar contains 7 active worksheets (L1-L4, L6-L7, L9-L10) plus two merger redirects (L5 and L8 into L4). Here is the recommended sequencing:

  **Order**   **Worksheet**                           **Level**     **Purpose**

  1           L1: Skills and Gaps Diagnostic          Level 1       Foundation. Maps skills, identifies gaps, creates team gap map with internal expertise.

  2           L4: Learning Resources & Engagement     Level 1       Selects and organises resources. Three-filter sort reduces decision fatigue.

  3           L3: Learning Journal                    Level 1       Individual practice. Daily reflection habit that reinforces learning retention.

  4           L6: Accountability in Learning          Level 1       Accountability structure. Learning contracts and partner check-ins.

  5           L2: Peer-to-Peer Learning               Level 1       Ongoing sessions. Uses L1 gap map to match teachers with learners.

  6           L7: Real-World Application              Level 2       Transfer design. Bridges learning to work with implementation intentions.

  7           L9: Tracking Learning Progress          Level 1       Progress visibility. Personal dashboards and manager check-in integration.

  \*          L10: Equitable Learning Opportunities   Level 2       Equity audit. Run when CLOVER ERA data shows uneven learning distribution.

L10 is sequenced separately because it is triggered by specific equity signals rather than being part of the standard learning development path. L1 through L9 form a natural progression from diagnostic to skill-building to application to tracking. L2 (Peer-to-Peer Learning) is ongoing rather than one-off: schedule regular sessions after the initial setup.
