| **RETIREMENT NOTE**                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   |
|                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                       |
| Retired. Organisational culture integration is the cumulative outcome of running R1 through R14 well, not a standalone exercise a manager can facilitate. If reflection is practised consistently (R1, R8), produces outcomes (R14), is modelled by leaders (R13), and is balanced (R6), it becomes culture. A workshop about making reflection part of the culture is redundant if the practice is already embedded. |

Reflection Pillar Summary

The complete Reflection pillar contains 9 active worksheets (R1-R6, R8, R13-R14) plus merger/retirement redirects for R7, R9-R12, R15. Recommended sequencing:

  **Order**   **Worksheet**                         **Level**    **Purpose**

  1           R1: Micro-Reflection Practice         Level 1      Foundation. Daily 2-5 minute habit with anchor point and format selection.

  2           R4: Structured Reflection Templates   Level 1      Resource. Four templates for deeper weekly/project reflection.

  3           R6: Balanced Reflections              Level 1      Quality control. 2:1 ratio prevents forced positivity or negativity spirals.

  4           R3: Reflection Buddy System           Level 1      Accountability. Paired weekly check-ins to sustain practice.

  5           R2: From Ideas to Action              Level 1      The bridge. Implementation intentions convert insights into behaviour change.

  6           R5: Feedback Integration              Level 1      Application. Structured second-pass processing of received feedback.

  7           R14: Linking to Outcomes              Level 2      Proof of value. Tracks reflection-to-outcome connections. Monthly showcase.

  8           R13: Engaging Leadership              Level 2      Leader modelling. Three leadership reflection questions. Visible practice.

  9           R8: Consistency Across Teams          Level 2      Organisational alignment. Cross-team minimum standard and insight sharing.

The sequence builds from individual habit (R1) through quality and accountability (R4, R6, R3) to action conversion (R2, R5) to visible impact (R14). R13 and R8 are leadership and organisational exercises that sit above the team level and should be run once the foundation is solid. R1 is the non-negotiable starting point: without the daily habit, nothing else in this pillar has raw material to work with.

worksheets.title: Vulnerability Circle
worksheets.forWhat: low vulnerability scores, declining trust, reluctance to raise issues, reluctance to admit mistakes
worksheets.lede: When someone shares something vulnerable and the group responds with acceptance rather than judgment, the brain releases oxytocin (the trust chemical) and dials down cortisol (the stress hormone). The amygdala, your brain's threat detector, recalibrates: it learns that this group is safe.
worksheets.body:
# V1: Vulnerability Circle

## Why This Works

When someone shares something vulnerable and the group responds with acceptance rather than judgment, the brain releases oxytocin (the trust chemical) and dials down cortisol (the stress hormone). The amygdala, your brain's threat detector, recalibrates: it learns that this group is safe.

This is not a one-time effect. Each positive vulnerability exchange strengthens the neural pathways associated with trust. Over time, the team's baseline threat response lowers, making collaboration, risk-taking, and honest communication easier at a biological level.

The reverse is also true. In teams where vulnerability is punished or ignored, cortisol stays elevated, the amygdala stays on alert, and people default to self-protection: withholding ideas, hiding mistakes, avoiding difficult conversations.

**If a team member asks "Why are we doing this?"**

> "Our brains are wired to protect us from social risk. That's useful, but it also means we hold back ideas, avoid tough conversations, and hide mistakes. This exercise helps the team build enough trust that we can lower those defences. The research shows that teams who practice this kind of openness make better decisions, catch problems earlier, and perform at a higher level."

## Before You Begin

### Materials

| In-Person | Remote |
|-----------|--------|
| Sticky notes (one pad per person) | Miro board (pre-set with sections) or Teams/Zoom chat |
| Pens | Digital timer (share screen) |
| Flipchart or whiteboard | Breakout rooms configured (pairs) |
| Timer visible to room | Camera on (strongly recommended) |

### Psychological Safety Check

> **Do NOT run this exercise if any of the following are true:**
>
> - The team has experienced layoffs, restructuring, or significant personnel changes within the past 3 weeks
> - There is an active, unresolved conflict between team members that has not been addressed
> - A team member is currently on a performance improvement plan (discuss with HR whether their participation is appropriate)
> - You (the manager) are not prepared to be vulnerable first
>
> If in doubt, start with V8 (Balancing Personal and Professional Vulnerability) as a lighter entry point.

### Manager Self-Preparation

Before facilitating this exercise, prepare your own vulnerability share. You will go first. This is non-negotiable: if the manager does not model vulnerability, the team will not follow.

Your share should be:

- Genuine (not rehearsed to the point of feeling safe and polished)
- Work-relevant (a professional struggle, a mistake, something you found difficult)
- Appropriately bounded (not a personal crisis or something that would make your team worry about your competence)
- Recent enough to feel real (not a story from 10 years ago that has been fully resolved)

**Calibration Guide:**

- **Too safe:** "I sometimes struggle with time management." (Everyone says this. It costs nothing.)
- **Right level:** "Last month I made a call on the project timeline that I now think was wrong, and I didn't flag it early enough because I didn't want to look like I didn't have it under control."
- **Too much:** "I'm not sure I'm the right person to be managing this team." (Creates anxiety rather than trust.)

## The Exercise

### Phase 1: Opening (5 minutes)

**What to say:**

> "Today we're going to do something different. I'm going to ask everyone, including me, to share something that we normally keep to ourselves at work. This isn't about therapy or oversharing. It's about building the kind of trust where we can be honest with each other about the things that actually matter."
>
> "Everything shared in this room stays in this room. There are no right or wrong answers. And I'm going to go first."

Set the ground rules:

- Confidentiality: nothing shared leaves this room
- No advice-giving: we listen, we acknowledge, we do not fix
- No judgment: verbal or nonverbal (watch for eye-rolls, crossed arms, phone-checking)
- Participation is encouraged but not forced: anyone can pass

### Phase 2: Manager Models (5 minutes)

Share your prepared vulnerability. Aim for 60-90 seconds. Do not over-explain or add a tidy resolution. End with something honest, not a lesson learned.

**What to say (after your share):**

> "That felt uncomfortable to say out loud. And that's kind of the point. I wanted to go first because I think it's important that you see me being honest about the things I find difficult, not just the things I've figured out."

**Facilitation note:** After you share, pause. Do not immediately invite others to share. Let the silence sit for 5-8 seconds. This pause signals that you are not performing; you meant it. The team is processing both the content and the fact that their manager just did something unexpected.

### Phase 3: Individual Preparation (5 minutes)

Give each person time to prepare their share privately. This is critical: asking people to share cold produces either refusal or performative responses.

**What to say:**

> "I'd like you to take 5 minutes to think about something you'd be willing to share. It could be a work challenge you've been sitting with, a mistake you haven't talked about, or something you're finding difficult right now. Write it down for yourself. You'll decide what you want to share out loud, and how much."

During this time: stay quiet. Do not walk around. Do not check your phone. Sit with the same discomfort you're asking them to sit with.

### Phase 4: Sharing Round (20-30 minutes)

Invite volunteers rather than going round-robin. Forced sharing creates resentment; volunteering builds genuine trust.

**What to say:**

> "Who'd like to go next? There's no order. Take your time."

After each share, the manager's response follows the same pattern:

1. Acknowledge: "Thank you for sharing that." (Genuine, brief.)
2. Validate: name what you heard without interpreting. "It sounds like that's been weighing on you" or "That took courage to say."
3. Do NOT: give advice, relate it to your own experience, or try to solve it.
4. Invite the group: "Does anyone want to respond?" (If the group adds supportive comments, let it flow naturally. If not, move on. Do not force connection.)

**What if someone passes?** Respect it completely. "No problem at all. Thank you." Move on without hesitation or visible disappointment. Checking in privately afterward is fine: "I just wanted to make sure you're okay. No pressure to share anything." A pass is not a failure. It may mean the trust is not yet there, or the timing is wrong, or the person is processing something they are not ready to voice. All of these are valid.

### Phase 5: Synthesis (5-10 minutes)

Do not ask "what did you learn?" This creates pressure to produce a neat takeaway from an emotional exercise. Instead:

**What to say:**

> "I want to thank everyone for what was shared today. I'm not going to ask you to summarise or draw conclusions. What I am going to ask is one simple question: having heard all of that, is there anything you'd do differently going forward?"
>
> Pause. Let responses come naturally. If none come, that is fine. Say: "That's okay. Sometimes the most important changes happen quietly."

### Phase 6: Close (2-3 minutes)

**What to say:**

> "What happened in this room stays in this room. What I'd ask is that you carry the spirit of it forward. If you're struggling with something, or you see a colleague struggling, let's make it easier to say so."
>
> "I'm going to follow up with each of you individually over the next week. Not to check up on you, just to check in."

Then end the meeting. Do not add agenda items or transition to other business. The exercise needs its own container.

## Facilitation Notes

In addition to the five standard contingencies (silence, emotional escalation, dominant participant, topic avoidance, performative compliance), this exercise has the following specific risks:

| Situation | Response |
|-----------|----------|
| Someone shares something that suggests they need professional support (e.g., mental health, harassment, safety) | Do not try to counsel them. Acknowledge what they said. After the session, speak to them privately: "I'm glad you shared that. I want to make sure you get the right support. Can I connect you with [HR/EAP/appropriate resource]?" If you believe there is an immediate safety concern, follow your organisation's safeguarding protocols. |
| Someone uses the exercise to criticise another team member (directly or indirectly) | Redirect immediately but without shaming: "I hear that this is a frustration. For this exercise, let's keep the focus on our own experiences rather than others' behaviour. We can address team dynamics separately." Follow up privately with both parties after the session. |
| The shares are all surface-level and safe ("I sometimes find meetings frustrating") | This is not a failure for a first session. Surface-level sharing in round one is the amygdala doing its job. Do not push for depth. Run the exercise again in 4-6 weeks. Depth increases with repeated exposure to safety. If you want to gently invite more depth: after a surface share, say "Thank you. Is there anything underneath that you'd be comfortable adding?" Accept whatever answer you get. |
| One person's share triggers a strong reaction in another person | This can happen when someone's vulnerability resonates deeply with another team member. Acknowledge it: "It looks like that connected with you. Would you like to say something, or would you prefer to sit with it?" Do not pressure them to explain their reaction. Check in privately afterward. |

## Signs This Is Working

| Timeframe | What to Look For |
|-----------|------------------|
| During the session | Shares become progressively more honest as the round continues. Body language shifts from guarded (arms crossed, leaning back) to open. People make eye contact with the speaker rather than looking at the floor. Spontaneous supportive comments from other team members (not prompted by you). |
| Within 1-2 weeks | A team member raises a concern or mistake in a regular meeting that they would previously have kept quiet. Conversations between team members feel slightly less guarded. Someone references the session positively ("like we talked about in that exercise"). |
| CLOVER ERA data (2-4 weeks) | Vulnerability pillar scores increase. Qualitative responses show language around trust, openness, or safety. Communication scores may also lift (vulnerability and communication are tightly linked). |
| Red flags | If vulnerability scores DROP after the exercise, the session may have felt unsafe to some participants. Action: follow up individually with each team member. Ask "How did that exercise land for you?" and listen without defending. |

## Remote/Hybrid Adaptation

| Element | Remote Modification |
|---------|-------------------|
| Cameras | Strongly request cameras on. Frame it as: "I'm asking everyone to have cameras on for this session so we can see each other. It matters for this kind of conversation." Do not force it. |
| Preparation phase | Use a private Miro board or ask people to write in their own notebook. The chat function is NOT appropriate for sensitive content, as it creates a permanent record. |
| Sharing round | Keep the full group together (no breakout rooms). The manager needs to be present for every share to manage the emotional tone. Mute notifications and close other applications. Ask participants to do the same. |
| After-session check-in | Individual check-ins are even more important remotely, as you lose the informal corridor conversations that happen naturally after an in-person session. Schedule 10-minute one-to-ones within the following week. |
| Timing | Add 10-15 minutes to total time. Online sessions need longer preparation time and more deliberate transitions between phases. |

## Cross-Pillar Connections

| Worksheet | Connection | Direction |
|-----------|------------|-----------|
| V2: Failure Stories | Builds on the trust established in V1 by focusing specifically on sharing professional mistakes. | Run after V1 (allow 2-4 weeks gap) |
| V8: Balancing Vulnerability | A lighter alternative if the team is not ready for V1. Covers boundary-setting and appropriate levels of sharing. | Can be run before V1 as a warm-up for cautious teams |
| C9: Conflict Communication | Vulnerability is a prerequisite for honest conflict resolution. Teams that have not done V1 will struggle with C9. | Run V1 before C9 |
| C15: Feedback Culture | Giving and receiving honest feedback requires the trust that V1 establishes. | Run V1 before C15 |
| R1: Micro-Reflection | Reflection prompts can reinforce vulnerability practice between sessions. | Complementary (run alongside) |

worksheets.title: Failure Stories
worksheets.forWhat: Low vulnerability scores, fear of admitting mistakes, blame culture signals, low innovation/risk-taking indicators
worksheets.lede: Share your prepared failure story. Keep it to 90 seconds. Follow the four-part structure: goal, what went wrong, cost, what changed.
worksheets.body:
# V2: Failure Stories

**Pillar**          **Vulnerability**                                        **Difficulty**           **Level 2**

  **Time Required**   40-50 minutes                                            **Group Size**           4-10 (optimal: 6-8)

  **Mode**            Team facilitation                                        **Format**               In-person or remote

  **Prerequisites**   V1 (Vulnerability Circle) recommended but not required   **CLOVER ERA Trigger**   Low vulnerability scores, fear of admitting mistakes, blame culture signals, low innovation/risk-taking indicators

## Why This Works

| **THE NEUROSCIENCE**                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                 |
|                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      |
| Fear of failure is a cortisol-driven response. When the brain associates failure with social punishment (criticism, loss of status, career consequences), the amygdala flags risk-taking as a threat. Over time, this creates teams that play it safe, hide mistakes, and avoid experimentation.                                                                                     |
|                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      |
| Sharing failure stories in a structured, safe context reverses this pattern. When someone shares a failure and receives acceptance rather than judgment, cortisol drops and oxytocin rises. The brain recategorises failure from 'threat' to 'survivable.' Repeated exposure to this reframing builds neural pathways that support risk-taking and honest reporting of problems. |
|                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      |
| The key mechanism is normalisation. When the manager and multiple team members share failures openly, the brain stops treating failure as an outlier event that singles you out and starts treating it as a shared human experience.                                                                                                                                                 |

| **IF A TEAM MEMBER ASKS "WHY ARE WE DOING THIS?"**                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    |
|                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                         |
| "We learn more from what goes wrong than from what goes right. But most teams bury their failures, which means they keep making the same mistakes and nobody dares try anything new. This exercise makes it normal to talk about what didn't work so we can actually learn from it." |

## Before You Begin

**Materials**

| **In-Person**                     | **Remote**                                         |

| Flipchart or whiteboard           | Miro board with pre-set story template sections    |
|                                   |                                                    |
| Markers                           | Digital timer (shared screen)                      |
|                                   |                                                    |
| Index cards (one per person)      | Private chat or DM function disabled during shares |
|                                   |                                                    |
| Timer                             | Camera on (recommended)                            |

| **PSYCHOLOGICAL SAFETY CHECK**                                                                                                                                                                                  |
|                                                                                                                                                                                                                 |
| Do NOT run this exercise if:                                                                                                                                                                                    |
|                                                                                                                                                                                                                 |
| • A team member has recently experienced a significant, visible failure that has not been resolved (the exercise would feel targeted)                                                                           |
|                                                                                                                                                                                                                 |
| • There is an active blame culture where mistakes lead to consequences (the exercise will produce performative stories, not real ones)                                                                          |
|                                                                                                                                                                                                                 |
| • The manager has not prepared their own failure story to share first                                                                                                                                           |
|                                                                                                                                                                                                                 |
| If the team has not completed V1 (Vulnerability Circle), consider the trust level carefully. V2 asks people to share specific failures, which requires more trust than the general vulnerability sharing in V1. |

**Manager Self-Preparation**

You go first. Prepare a professional failure story that follows this structure:

-   What you were trying to do (the goal, not the context lecture)

-   What went wrong (specific, not vague)

-   What it cost (be honest about the impact, do not minimise)

-   What you took from it (not a tidy lesson, but what actually changed in how you work)

| **CALIBRATION GUIDE**                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                |
|                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      |
| Too safe: "I once missed a deadline." (Too common, too low-stakes. Nobody learns anything.)                                                                                                                                                                                        |
|                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      |
| Right level: "I pushed a project decision through without consulting the team because I was sure I was right. It turned out I was missing critical information that two team members had. We lost three weeks of work and I had to rebuild trust with the people I'd overridden." |
|                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      |
| Too much: "I was nearly fired for\..." (Shifts the tone from learning to crisis narrative.)                                                                                                                                                                                        |

## The Exercise

### Phase 1: Opening and Framing (5 minutes)

| **WHAT TO SAY**                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  |
|                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  |
| "Today I'm going to ask each of us to share a time we got something wrong at work. Not a small thing. Something that actually mattered. The goal is not to dwell on mistakes. The goal is to make it normal to talk about them, because teams that can do that catch problems earlier, learn faster, and take smarter risks." |
|                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  |
| "I'm going to go first. Then I'll give you a few minutes to think about your own story before we go round."                                                                                                                                                                                                                  |

### Phase 2: Manager Models (3-4 minutes)

Share your prepared failure story. Keep it to 90 seconds. Follow the four-part structure: goal, what went wrong, cost, what changed.

| **FACILITATION NOTE**                                                                                                                                                                                                                        |
|                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              |
| Resist the urge to wrap your story with a redemption arc. "And then I learned to always consult my team and everything was better" kills the authenticity. End on what changed, honestly. If you still struggle with it sometimes, say so. |

### Phase 3: Individual Preparation (5 minutes)

| **WHAT TO SAY**                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          |
|                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          |
| "Take five minutes to think about a professional failure you'd be willing to share. Use these four prompts: What were you trying to do? What went wrong? What did it cost? What did you take from it? Write it down for yourself. You'll decide how much detail you share out loud." |

Give each person an index card with the four prompts pre-printed (or display on screen for remote). Writing forces specificity. Thinking alone often stays vague.

### Phase 4: Sharing Round (20-25 minutes)

Invite volunteers. Do not go round-robin. Allow 2-3 minutes per story.

After each story, the manager's response:

5.  Acknowledge: "Thank you. That's a real one."

6.  Ask one follow-up (optional): "What's the thing you wish you'd done differently in the moment?" This invites reflection without judgment.

7.  Do NOT: say "I had a similar experience" (makes it about you) or "At least you learned from it" (minimises the cost).

8.  Invite the group briefly: "Does that connect with anyone else's experience?" Short responses only. This is not a group therapy session.

| **ENERGY MANAGEMENT**                                                                                                                                                                                                                                           |
|                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                 |
| Stories 3-4 often dip in energy as the novelty wears off. If you notice this, after story 3, say: "I'm hearing a pattern here. Can anyone name what connects these stories?" This shifts from passive listening to active synthesis and re-engages the room. |

### Phase 5: Pattern Recognition (5-7 minutes)

This is where the individual stories become team learning. Do not skip this phase.

| **WHAT TO SAY**                                                                                                                                                                                                                                       |
|                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                       |
| "Now I want us to look at what we just heard as a collection, not individual stories. What patterns do you notice? Are there common causes? Common pressures? Things that our team or our organisation does that makes these failures more likely?" |

Write the patterns on the flipchart/Miro. Common ones: time pressure leading to shortcuts, not asking for help early enough, assumptions going unchallenged, information not reaching the right people.

Then the critical question:

| **WHAT TO SAY**                                                                                                      |
|                                                                                                                      |
| "Looking at these patterns, which one is most alive for us right now? Which one are we most at risk of repeating?" |

This question moves the exercise from reflection to prevention. It is the most valuable moment of the session.

### Phase 6: Close (3 minutes)

| **WHAT TO SAY**                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                             |
|                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                             |
| "What happened here stays here, but the patterns don't have to. If you see one of these patterns showing up in our work, I want you to name it. You can say 'I think we're doing the thing' and everyone will know what that means. That's the goal: catching the pattern before it becomes the next failure story." |

## Facilitation Notes

| **Situation**                                                                                    | **Response**                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  |

| **Someone shares a failure they clearly haven't processed (still angry, still blaming others)** | Acknowledge without redirecting too sharply: "I can hear that this one still stings. Thank you for bringing it." Do not correct their framing in the group. If you hear blame rather than ownership, let it stand in the session. Address it privately afterward if needed. |
|                                                                                                  |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                               |
|                                                                                                  | The group will notice the difference between this story and the others. That contrast is itself a learning moment.                                                                                                                                                            |

| **Stories stay safe and inconsequential ("I once sent an email to the wrong person")**         | After 2-3 safe stories, recalibrate gently: "These are useful. Can I push us slightly? Think about a time when you made a decision that had real consequences. Something that changed how you work."                                                                        |
|                                                                                                  |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                               |
|                                                                                                  | If the group still stays surface, accept it. This is a trust signal. Run V1 first next time.                                                                                                                                                                                  |

| **Someone shares a failure that implicates another person in the room**                          | Redirect immediately: "Let's keep the focus on our own decisions and actions. What was the part that was in your control?" This reframes without shaming either party.                                                                                                     |
|                                                                                                  |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                               |
|                                                                                                  | Follow up privately with both people after the session.                                                                                                                                                                                                                       |

| **The manager's own failure story falls flat (no reaction, awkward silence)**                   | This usually means the story was either too safe or too polished. Do not try to fix it in the moment. Move to the preparation phase. For next time, recalibrate using the calibration guide.                                                                                  |

## Signs This Is Working

| **Timeframe**                   | **What to Look For**                                                                                                                                                                          |

| **During the session**          | Stories become more specific and honest as the round progresses                                                                                                                               |
|                                 |                                                                                                                                                                                               |
|                                 | Someone says "I've never told anyone at work about this"                                                                                                                                   |
|                                 |                                                                                                                                                                                               |
|                                 | The pattern recognition phase generates genuine debate rather than polite agreement                                                                                                           |

| **Within 1-2 weeks**            | A team member raises a problem or mistake in a meeting without waiting for it to escalate                                                                                                     |
|                                 |                                                                                                                                                                                               |
|                                 | Language shifts: "I got this wrong" instead of "there was a problem with\..."                                                                                                             |
|                                 |                                                                                                                                                                                               |
|                                 | Someone references the patterns from the session in a work context                                                                                                                            |

| **CLOVER ERA data (2-4 weeks)** | Vulnerability scores increase                                                                                                                                                                 |
|                                 |                                                                                                                                                                                               |
|                                 | Communication scores may also improve (failure sharing opens other honest conversations)                                                                                                      |
|                                 |                                                                                                                                                                                               |
|                                 | Qualitative data shows language about learning, honesty, or mistakes                                                                                                                          |

| **Red flags**                   | If vulnerability scores drop or people seem more guarded after the session, the safety conditions may not have been met. Follow up individually. Ask: "How did that exercise land for you?" |

## Remote/Hybrid Adaptation

  **Element**               **Remote Modification**

  **Preparation cards**     Display the four-prompt structure on a shared screen. Ask people to write privately in a notebook, NOT in chat or a shared document.

  **Sharing round**         Keep full group (no breakout rooms). The manager must be present for every share. Ask everyone to close other applications and focus.

  **Pattern recognition**   Use Miro sticky notes for patterns instead of flipchart. This gives remote participants equal input (typing is faster than waiting for airtime).

  **Cameras**               Strongly request cameras on for this session. Seeing faces during vulnerability matters.

  **Timing**                Add 10 minutes. Online sharing rounds take longer because speakers pause more without physical feedback cues.

## Cross-Pillar Connections

  **Worksheet**                      **Connection**                                                                                                           **Direction**

  **V1: Vulnerability Circle**       V1 builds the trust foundation that V2 requires. V2 focuses specifically on failure rather than general vulnerability.   Run V1 before V2 (2-4 weeks gap)

  **V7: Fear of Failure**            V7 addresses the systemic conditions that create fear of failure. V2 addresses the personal experience of failure.       Complementary (run within same month)

  **V10: Respectful Disagreement**   Failure stories often reveal moments where challenge or disagreement was needed but did not happen.                      Run after V2

  **R2: From Ideas to Action**       The pattern recognition phase in V2 generates insights that need action planning to become real change.                  Complementary

worksheets.body:
# V3: Structured Feedback Exchange

*Formerly: Feedback Roulette. Rebuilt from scratch. The original anonymous bowl mechanic created anxiety without support. This version provides psychological safety through structure.*

  **Pillar**          **Vulnerability**                                **Difficulty**           **Level 3**

  **Time Required**   50-60 minutes                                    **Group Size**           4-8 (optimal: 6)

  **Mode**            Team facilitation                                **Format**               In-person preferred

  **Prerequisites**   V1 (Vulnerability Circle) strongly recommended   **CLOVER ERA Trigger**   Low feedback culture scores, difficulty giving/receiving feedback, avoidance of constructive criticism

## Why This Works

| **THE NEUROSCIENCE**                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                |
|                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                     |
| Receiving feedback activates the brain's threat detection system. The amygdala scans incoming feedback for social danger: Am I being judged? Is my status at risk? Will this affect my standing in the group? When feedback arrives without warning, without context, or without safety, cortisol spikes and the prefrontal cortex (rational thinking) goes offline. The person hears the threat, not the content. |
|                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                     |
| Structured feedback reverses this. When the recipient knows what to expect, has time to prepare, and feels in control of the process, the prefrontal cortex stays engaged. The brain can process the feedback as information rather than threat. Adding positive feedback alongside constructive feedback activates dopamine reward circuits, making the whole experience feel more balanced.                       |
|                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                     |
| The original Feedback Roulette format (anonymous notes in a bowl, random distribution) maximised threat signals: no control, no context, no relationship. This rebuilt version prioritises the relationship between giver and receiver.                                                                                                                                                                             |

| **IF A TEAM MEMBER ASKS "WHY ARE WE DOING THIS?"**                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                       |
|                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            |
| "Most of us have never been taught how to give or receive feedback in a way that actually lands. We either avoid it entirely or deliver it badly. This exercise lets us practise both in a structured, safe way so that feedback becomes a normal part of how we work together, not something we dread." |

## Before You Begin

| **PSYCHOLOGICAL SAFETY CHECK**                                                                              |
|                                                                                                             |
| This is a Level 3 exercise. Do NOT run it if:                                                               |
|                                                                                                             |
| • The team has not completed V1 or equivalent trust-building work                                           |
|                                                                                                             |
| • There are unresolved interpersonal conflicts that could hijack the feedback process                       |
|                                                                                                             |
| • The team has a history of feedback being used punitively (in performance reviews, in public settings)     |
|                                                                                                             |
| • Anyone on the team is in a probation period or performance management process                             |
|                                                                                                             |
| If any of these conditions exist, start with V8 (Balancing Vulnerability) and C15 (Feedback Culture) first. |

**Pre-work (sent 48 hours before the session)**

Send each team member a simple brief: "In our next session, each person will give one piece of feedback to one other person, and receive one piece of feedback from someone else. You'll know who you're giving to, and you'll have time to prepare. The feedback should be work-related, specific, and constructive. Think about what would genuinely help the other person."

Assign feedback pairs. Every person gives to one person and receives from a different person. The manager participates as both giver and receiver. Pairings should be rotated if you run this exercise again.

## The Exercise

### Phase 1: Framing and Ground Rules (5 minutes)

| **WHAT TO SAY**                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                         |
|                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                         |
| "Today we're practising feedback as a skill. Not performance review feedback. Not criticism. Feedback as something we do for each other because we want each other to succeed."                                                                                      |
|                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                         |
| "Ground rules: the feedback you give should be specific, about work behaviour (not personality), and aimed at helping. The person receiving feedback listens fully, then responds with what they heard, not with a defence. We'll practise this structure together." |

### Phase 2: Feedback Structure Teaching (5 minutes)

Introduce the SBI framework on the flipchart/screen:

-   Situation: "In last week's project review meeting\..."

-   Behaviour: "\...you presented the data without context for the new team members\..."

-   Impact: "\...which meant they couldn't contribute to the discussion and two important questions went unasked."

Demonstrate with a live example. Give feedback to yourself, out loud, using SBI: "In yesterday's planning session, I moved through the agenda too quickly without checking whether people had questions. The impact was that two decisions got made without full input."

### Phase 3: Preparation (5 minutes)

Each person prepares their feedback using SBI. They write it down. Writing forces precision and reduces the chance of the feedback becoming vague or emotional in delivery.

### Phase 4: Feedback Exchange (25-30 minutes)

Each pair takes turns. The room stays together (no breakout rooms). This matters: the group witnessing feedback being given and received well normalises the practice.

Sequence for each exchange (3-4 minutes per pair):

9.  Giver delivers feedback using SBI structure.

10. Receiver pauses. Counts to three silently. Then responds: "What I heard was\..." (reflects back without defending).

11. Giver confirms or clarifies: "Yes, that's it" or "Not quite, what I meant was\..."

12. Receiver says: "Thank you. I'll think about that." Full stop. No explanation, no justification, no counter-feedback.

| **FACILITATION NOTE**                                                                                                                                                                                          |
|                                                                                                                                                                                                                |
| The hardest part for receivers is not defending. Coach this explicitly: "Your job right now is to hear it, not to respond to it. You'll have time to process later. For now, just listen and reflect back." |
|                                                                                                                                                                                                                |
| If a receiver starts defending, intervene gently: "Can I pause you there? Try just reflecting back what you heard first."                                                                                    |

### Phase 5: Debrief (10 minutes)

| **WHAT TO SAY**                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            |
|                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            |
| "We're not going to discuss the content of anyone's feedback. That's private between each pair. What I want to explore is the process. What was harder: giving or receiving? What was it like to reflect back without defending? What surprised you?" |

Let the debrief run naturally. The insights that emerge here are the real learning: people consistently report that receiving feedback is harder than giving it, and that the reflection step changed how they processed the content.

### Phase 6: Close (3 minutes)

| **WHAT TO SAY**                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                     |
|                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                     |
| "This was a structured exercise. Real feedback doesn't happen in a session like this. It happens in the moment, in the work. My ask is this: between now and our next team meeting, find one opportunity to give someone on this team a piece of feedback using the structure we practised. It doesn't have to be big. It just has to be real." |

## Facilitation Notes

| **Situation**                                                                            | **Response**                                                                                                                                                                                                                    |

| **Feedback becomes personal rather than behavioural ("You're always disorganised")**  | Intervene immediately but gently: "Can I help reframe that? Let's get specific. What's a recent situation where this showed up?" Guide them back to SBI.                                                                    |
|                                                                                          |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                 |
|                                                                                          | If the receiver is visibly hurt, acknowledge it: "That landed differently than intended. Let's reset and try again with a specific example."                                                                                 |

| **A receiver becomes defensive or argumentative**                                        | Redirect: "I can see this is landing. Let's come back to the structure. Right now, your only job is to reflect back what you heard." If they cannot, offer a break: "Take a moment. We can come back to this."             |
|                                                                                          |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                 |
|                                                                                          | Do NOT force the exchange to continue if the safety has been compromised.                                                                                                                                                       |

| **The feedback is too vague to be useful ("You're doing great, keep it up")**         | Coach in real time: "That's a good starting point. Can you make it more specific? What's one thing they did recently that you want to see more of?" This teaches specificity without embarrassing the giver.                |

| **Someone's feedback reveals a serious unresolved issue between them and the receiver** | Do not let it play out in the group. Acknowledge: "This sounds like something that needs a deeper conversation. Can the two of you set aside time this week to talk it through? I'm happy to facilitate if that would help." |
|                                                                                          |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                 |
|                                                                                          | Follow up to ensure the conversation happens.                                                                                                                                                                                   |

## Signs This Is Working

| **Timeframe**                   | **What to Look For**                                                                                                                                                   |

| **During the session**          | Receivers genuinely listen rather than preparing their rebuttal                                                                                                        |
|                                 |                                                                                                                                                                        |
|                                 | At least one person says "I didn't know that's how it landed"                                                                                                      |
|                                 |                                                                                                                                                                        |
|                                 | The debrief generates honest reflection about the difficulty of feedback                                                                                               |

| **Within 1-2 weeks**            | Someone gives unsolicited feedback using the SBI structure outside of the exercise                                                                                     |
|                                 |                                                                                                                                                                        |
|                                 | A team member asks for feedback rather than waiting to receive it                                                                                                      |
|                                 |                                                                                                                                                                        |
|                                 | Feedback references become normal rather than loaded ("Can I give you some quick feedback on that?")                                                                 |

| **CLOVER ERA data (2-4 weeks)** | Vulnerability scores increase                                                                                                                                          |
|                                 |                                                                                                                                                                        |
|                                 | Communication scores improve (feedback is a communication accelerator)                                                                                                 |
|                                 |                                                                                                                                                                        |
|                                 | Qualitative responses reference openness, honesty, or trust                                                                                                            |

| **Red flags**                   | If people avoid each other after the session or become more guarded, the exercise may have surfaced content that was not adequately contained. Follow up individually. |

## Remote/Hybrid Adaptation

  **Element**           **Remote Modification**

  **Exchange format**   Keep the full group on video. Do NOT use breakout rooms. The group witnessing the exchanges is part of the normalisation.

  **Preparation**       Use a private document or notebook. Never write feedback in shared digital spaces.

  **Nonverbal cues**    Ask receivers to nod or give a visible acknowledgment when they hear the feedback. Online, the giver cannot see body language as clearly and may interpret silence as rejection.

  **Timing**            Allow 4-5 minutes per pair instead of 3-4. The reflection-back step takes longer online without physical proximity cues.

## Cross-Pillar Connections

  **Worksheet**                        **Connection**                                                                                       **Direction**

  **V1: Vulnerability Circle**         V1 builds the trust that makes V3 possible. Without trust, feedback exchange becomes performative.   Run V1 before V3 (2+ weeks gap)

  **C15: Feedback Culture**            C15 addresses the systemic conditions for feedback. V3 provides the practice. They work as a pair.   Run C15 before or alongside V3

  **V8: Balancing Vulnerability**      If V3 is too intense for the team, V8 is a gentler entry point.                                      Alternative entry if V1 has not been completed

  **L6: Accountability in Learning**   Feedback is a key input for learning accountability. V3 establishes the skill.                       Complementary
